title: How can collaboration across user-centred design teams support complex digital delivery?

content.content: People do not experience justice services as fragmented products or user flows. While we have to create artificial product boundaries and team divides to deliver a service, the experience of the end user does not mirror these divides. In real life, people’s journeys cross different systems and processes. Improving one part in isolation is rarely enough.

Beneath that cohesive experience, at the heart of MoJ service transformation, is complexity. How can digital service delivery at its best simplify complexity at a strategic level and create smooth, unified experiences?
What Really is Complexity?

According to systems thinking, complexity describes interconnected systems. The difference between a complex system and a complicated one is predictability. Interconnectivity is complicated when connected parts impact each other predictably. Contrastingly, the behaviour of complex elements and how they will affect each other is often unpredictable, with change emerging over time. Outcomes can never be entirely known.
Let’s Get Strategic: Smarter not Harder

There is a principle in UX law that systems come to mirror the team structures that build them, known colloquially as the ‘pants over trousers’ rule. Similarly, it’s easy for this to occur in reverse: methods come to mirror system complexity. Teams introduce many varied, tactical solutions with a whack-a-mole effect, rather than stepping back and looking at wider strategy.

Thanks to their brilliance, our teams tackle this complexity skilfully and willingly. However, we understand that it’s inevitable among proactive teams that solutions-at-speed pop up that are tactical, rather than strategic: Localised, short-term improvements in isolated areas can lead to the creation of new issues, potentially taking a toll on efficiency and even wellbeing.
So, which strategic initiatives support complexity? Here are a few we have found work well…
End-to-End Research Benefits All

Historically, the Crime Applications service consisted of several, siloed product teams, some on legacy and some on newly transformed parts of the product. User researchers from four teams collaborated to design usability testing for the entire end-to-end journey across both legacy and transformed services.
End-to-end insight revealed previously unseen offline tasks, which were then prioritised and incorporated into the digital journey.

Ultimately, this uncovered how the products work together as one, rather than in isolation, replicating how they are really experienced. The result was not only a more cohesive and consistent experience. The initiative encouraged closer ways of working between teams, who continue to develop a shared strategy to improve the end-to-end journey holistically.
Dig a Little Deeper: root-causes

Bringing teams together can take different shapes and forms. When challenges and blockers have come to seem intractable, we have found the Five Why workshop format allows us to come together and collectively uncover root causes. The format moves beyond the obvious issue by repeatedly asking ‘why?’ to get closer to the underlying cause. It follows basic if/then logic, applying cause-and-effect thinking.

We recently joined two teams together, where one team represented user submissions and the other represented users assessing submissions. Merging the teams meant both sides of the service interaction could be considered as one whole and allowed for closer collaboration. During the merger, we ran a Five Whys workshop to better understand the root causes where collaboration had created delays or uncertainty. This helped us understand where the real gaps were and how they connected across the service, rather than looking for a solution within a single team.
Single-Source-of-Truth
Wherever possible, we try to create a single source of truth to support collective understanding at a higher-level.

Recently within Legal Aid Agency Digital (LAAD), we collaborated with policy colleagues to create detailed journey maps of the crime and civil end-to-end. This has supported conversations between policy, digital and operations to decide which steps in the process are ripe for 'simplification', change that requires not just a new digital skin but changes to the rules that govern things. Our researchers and service designers combined our disparate insights into one map, which they shared among different disciplines across the business to both validate and discuss implications.

Creating a ‘visual map’ like this enables us to demonstrate impact on users more effectively than written reports. Senior stakeholders can see the ‘headlines’ at a glance. Similarly, a single service blueprint is invaluable, even more so when it includes issues experienced by users. A single log of user needs allows strategic needs (those that shape real product change) to be highlighted.
Powerful Insights

The Justice Research team is creating a central research repository, using AI to bring insights from across the organisation together. The aim is to enable us to look across services, agencies and teams to understand common, powerful themes and issues across the justice system.

However sometimes holistic insight is a happy side-effect. Wherever possible we have tried to centre cross-cutting activities around knowledge-share that actively strengthens collective insight, which in turn enhances cohesive product quality.

Cross-cutting Justice Design Crits, for example, have the incidental benefit of requiring people to share why they would suggest certain improvements, whether it’s due to previously little-known caseworker way-of-working or a provider need. As a result, group understanding of justice users grows together, as well as embedding that group intelligence into the product. People become a guardrail for quality.
Beyond Artificial Siloes

To get a complex usable product across the line it’s necessary to be product orientated. However, this can lead us to overlook the fact that digital products play only a small - and hopefully supportive - part in rich, real experiences.

To combat this, over the last nine months in LAAD, we have established a small working group whose aim is to understand how the LAAD product is experienced, as a whole. The group consists of one service designer and two user researchers with the benefit of working primarily outside product teams. Their insights are not constrained to product silos and instead reflect the holistic way end users truly access a product.

This helps us think beyond product boundaries and identify opportunities for service transformation that we may not have previously identified. The team is identifying gaps in our understanding as an organisation, prioritising those discovery opportunities with the greatest potential for impact.
‘Beta’ is Better than Never (and Sooner is Best!)

Kicking off these types of initiatives sooner rather than later has several perks. Discovery is exponentially richer, more insightful and impactful. Teams grow together and are more adaptable to change.

Laying down a stable foundation ensures quality later. Activities like exploratory end-too-end research and root cause analysis give teams the opportunity to think slow, as well as fast. Implementing them from the start creates cohesion of both insight and people.
What’s the golden thread across these examples? A holistic view is invaluable.

It is a common sentiment that simplifying complexity is part of user-centred design; but we cannot do that without stepping out of the weeds to identify how parts of the user experience connect and to scan for what is being overlooked. It is often only a bird’s eye view that allows you to see the most impactful, simple solutions that align with the daily lives of users.

title: From the classroom to code - Why it is never too late to be curious

content.content: National STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) Day 2026 takes place on 8th November and the focus is on innovation—challenging us to ask questions, solve problems, and build something new.

For Lauren, curiosity and the willingness to try something completely new have taken her from primary school teaching and running her own photography business, to starting a new career in technology through the GFiE Pathways to STEM scheme at the Intellectual Property Office (IPO).
Lauren’s journey shows that there is no single route into STEM, and that you do not need to have started your career in technology to build a future in it.
About Pathways to STEM

Pathways to STEM is a GFiE-accredited Pathway designed to help address STEM skills shortages across the Civil Service, while breaking down barriers to employment for people from underrepresented groups. Working with partners, the pathway creates accessible, skills-focused routes into STEM for people whose potential may not always be recognised through traditional recruitment routes.

Lauren’s journey is one example of the difference these opportunities can make. By focusing on potential and a willingness to learn, Pathways to STEM helps people from different backgrounds access opportunities, develop new skills and build careers in STEM that they may once have thought were out of reach.
If you are interested in using Pathways to STEM to recruit talented individuals into STEM roles for your department, please contact the Pathway to STEM Lead on GFiE@ipo.gov.uk

title: Inside our AI and Data accelerator: what we are learning from test and learn work in Barnsley

content.content: Rarely a day goes by without hearing the words ‘artificial intelligence’. From news reports to boardroom strategies to conversations during the daily commute, AI seems to be everywhere. And a day in government is no different.

Policymakers in Whitehall want to scale up AI adoption to transform public services. The Prime Minister's new AI Taskforce is the latest sign of this ambition. But we still know very little about what it actually takes to deploy and evaluate these technologies in the public sector.

Our Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) accelerator on AI and data for children’s services is trying to change that by working directly with local authorities to ‘test’ how AI can improve services before committing to rolling anything out at scale. The Government Outcomes Lab works as TLG’s independent learning and evaluation partner.

Clare and Ashna both work on the accelerator. Clare oversees the accelerators work day-to-day with Barnsley partners and Ashna brings her evaluation expertise - observing how the work evolves and feeding back learnings that could help others adapt and scale similar projects elsewhere. In this blog, they share three early learnings from Wave 1 of the accelerator’s work.
To see this work in action watch this video.
Why Barnsley, why now?

A local authority is where most citizens engage tangibly with the state. It is where families access essential services; from housing, education, health and social care, to benefits, tax, and safeguarding. But local authorities are busy, complex, multi-layered organisations.

The number of looked after children has increased 70% in 30 years, now consuming a quarter of Local Authority service budgets. In 2025, Barnsley had 56 children in external residential care placements, costing £0.5m per child a year in April 2026.

We know we want to improve public services so they work more efficiently, are better connected to local communities and improve lives. However, without testing an idea or plan using a prototype, it becomes impossible to know whether AI might play a valuable role, and the risks it might pose for residents accessing public services.

This accelerator is working closely with partners in Barnsley to explore whether council teams can use data and technology to take a more prevention-focused approach to service delivery, so that at-risk children and families in Barnsley receive the right support, at the right time and avoid care placements.

This work is also taking place as Barnsley becomes the UK’s first government-backed Tech Town. Tech Town is a partnership between central government, Barnsley Council and local organisations, set up to explore practical, AI use cases that originate in place. The ambition is for Barnsley to act as a trailblazer, testing how AI can tackle bespoke challenges in different sectors, and as a result, improve everyday life while keeping change rooted in local priorities, institutions and residents’ perspectives.

That work is already underway: from new AI skills and training programmes for residents, workers and businesses, including the AI Upskilling Challenge Fund and the AI Career Launchpad. Barnsley Council is also developing The Seam Digital Campus and National Centre for Digital Technologies, and offering programmes such as Ignite AI and Meld AI to help local businesses build the confidence and capability to use AI. Together, these Tech Town initiatives make up the wider context and local conditions in which the TLG Accelerator is working. For evaluation, it is important to monitor how this wider activity may influence the accelerator’s progress.
Three early lessons

After starting in December 2025, most of the accelerator’s early work involved conducting sessions with Barnsley Council and frontline services to understand the issue and design a clear roadmap for this work.
Learning 1: Defining the right problem to focus on takes time, and involves a lot of people and decision making

Working out the exact scope of the problem and finding the right people to talk to at different levels of a local authority is crucial. Before testing anything, the accelerator has recognised the value of doing relational work first:
The learning generated from this ‘discovery’ process has opened up more questions, such as:
Learning 2: Being willing to change course is a good thing, and perhaps the very essence of doing ‘test and learn’
A couple of months in, the accelerator made a deliberate decision to change focus and pivot from their original plans, which was improving productivity for frontline staff in the council.

This happened after several conversations and brainstorming exercises with place partners, who understood that frontline teams in Barnsley often work in crisis mode. The question became: could a more targeted, strategic intervention create change in an organisation constantly trapped in crisis?
They used this insight to shift the focus to strategic-level stakeholders, to help develop a shared ‘service delivery transformation ambition’ for the council.

Although this decision to pivot caused a temporary drop in confidence levels for the accelerator team, having this insight from frontline teams meant that this was valuable learning and a useful course-correction early in the process.
Learning 3: Data and AI solutions can’t be adopted in isolation from the wider institution

The accelerator’s own pace of technology adoption can only move as fast as the local authority - as an institution and system - is able to absorb it. Institutional practice and organisational culture matter just as much as the technology itself. For this accelerator, this has meant understanding:
Without understanding how their ‘test and learn’ work interacts with these local conditions, it is hard to say what is working and what needs to change.
Evaluating a moving target

As a team of evaluators, we are in a unique and unusual position. In traditional government evaluation, findings are often published at the end of a programme. The Government Outcomes Lab is part of a live TLG partnership, so we can share learning as we go, and the programme can act on it in real time.

This also makes us think carefully about our role in a programme where the work keeps evolving. What counts as good evidence? How do we balance the flexibility an agile accelerator needs with the rigour a robust evaluation demands? What outcomes should we hold a reform programme accountable for, when it's built on learning from failure as much as success? We'll return to this in a future post.
What’s coming next
A lot of what we have seen so far is likely to change as the accelerator’s work progresses.
We expect that insights from Barnsley will help us understand how to approach AI implementation in other regions and types of services.
Want to learn more or get involved?

Discover key lessons from the Test, Learn and Grow project in Barnsley—including why building strong relationships early matters, how to adapt when plans change, and why AI must fit into existing council processes.

title: UK providing specialist care to aid worker with Ebola

content.content: This post relates to an emerging incident and will be updated as new information becomes available
A British person has been diagnosed with Ebola after helping with the outbreak response in the DRC and has been brought to the UK for specialist treatment.

They have been safely transported back to the UK via medevac - a specialist flight during which an individual receives detailed medical care, and are now in one of the UK's High Consequence Infectious Disease (HCID) units at the Royal Free Hospital, London. HCID units are specialist NHS units designed to safely treat people diagnosed with rare and serious infections.

Large infectious disease outbreaks like the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) require a large scale, international response. Specialists from countries around the world are assisting on the ground in DRC. Outbreak responses like this one always carry risk of the infection spreading to those who are responding.

The risk to the UK public remains low. The UK has well-established systems, specialist facilities and highly trained staff for managing infectious diseases like Ebola. This post explains what is happening, how Ebola spreads and what you need to do.
Why is this person being medically evacuated and why can’t they remain in DRC for treatment?

The medical evacuation of a British worker with a high consequence infectious disease such as Ebola is part of our duty of care to those serving in challenging and high-risk environments overseas. This ensures the individual has access to specialist care within the UK health system, while being closer to family and other support networks during treatment and recovery.
This approach reflects the UK's commitment to supporting humanitarian workers who undertake difficult and important work on behalf of vulnerable communities around the world.
Due to the precautions taken, this medical evacuation will not increase the risk to the UK public.
Do I need to take any extra precautions?
No. The overall risk to the UK has not changed, and the patient is being treated in isolation. You do not need to take any extra precautions.
How is the specialist unit at the Royal Free Hospital different from an ordinary hospital ward?

The Royal Free Hospital has specialist high-level isolation beds and some of the best facilities in the world for treating unusual infectious diseases. The patient is being treated in isolation. This means there is minimal risk of Ebola spreading as a result of this case.
Staff in these units are highly trained and follow strict protocols to protect themselves, other NHS staff and the public.
Can Ebola spread to other people during a medevac transfer to the UK?

This is extremely unlikely. The patient was transported by highly trained specialists who wear full personal protective equipment (PPE) and follow strict infection control procedures throughout the journey.
How does Ebola spread?

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of a person who is sick with the virus, such as vomit, diarrhoea or blood. It is not airborne, so it cannot be caught from particles in the air. This makes it very different from infections such as flu and COVID-19, which spread much more easily through coughs and sneezes.

Healthcare workers caring for patients with Ebola wear full protective equipment when they are in close contact with a patient. This prevents the infection spreading by creating a barrier between the healthcare worker and the bodily fluids of an infected person.
What are the symptoms of Ebola, and how long do they take to appear?

Symptoms can appear between 2 and 21 days after coming into contact with the infection, and on average after 8 to 10 days. Illness usually starts suddenly with a fever, headache, tiredness, muscle pain and a sore throat. After a few days, symptoms such as nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting often follow.
Many other illnesses, such as malaria, cause similar symptoms which is much more common in returning travellers.
Is the NHS prepared?

The NHS has well-established processes for managing an Ebola case, including rapid testing and strict infection prevention and control in healthcare settings. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) provides clinical advice and testing to the NHS for viral haemorrhagic fevers, including Ebola, and has a test for the strain causing this outbreak in the DRC.
What should I do if I think I might have Ebola?
Unless you have visited an affected country and been in contact with the body fluids of an infected person, there is very little chance that you have Ebola.

If you have visited the DRC or other affected surrounding areas in the last 21 days and you become unwell with symptoms such as fever, chills, muscle aches, vomiting, diarrhoea or a sore throat, you should:
You should not go to a GP surgery or hospital without calling first.
Is there a vaccine or treatment?

There are currently no licensed vaccines or treatments for most species of Ebola virus, including the Bundibugyo strain causing the current outbreak. Vaccines and treatments exist for a different species of Ebola virus. Specialist teams will provide the patient with the best available supportive care.
I'm planning to travel to an affected area. What should I do?

If you are planning to visit an area affected by the current outbreak, think carefully about your plans and speak to a travel health specialist. You can find advice on the NaTHNaC Ebola disease page and from the FCDO.

Organisations sending workers to affected areas, where they may be exposed to Ebola through their work, should register them with the UKHSA Returning Workers Scheme. The scheme has been activated to protect and monitor the health of these workers. UKHSA is closely monitoring the situation and will provide updates if anything changes. A dedicated page on GOV.UK lists outbreaks and case locations of haemorrhagic fevers Ebola and Marburg.

title: Misleading reporting on the Overnight Visitor Levy

content.content: This week the government introduced the Visitor Levy Bill in Parliament, bringing local leaders a step closer to new powers to invest in the high streets, cultural sites and attractions that make communities great places to live, work and visit.
This was welcomed by almost a dozen mayors, as well as cultural organisations and academics.

However, there has been some misleading media reports claiming that accommodation providers face 14 years in jail for not paying the Overnight Visitor Levy and could have to repay it for up to 20 years.
The fact is, no one will go to prison for an honest mistake or a minor breach like an occasional error when collecting the levy.

Just as is the case for other charges, like VAT, prison would only be considered in the most serious cases, including where the levy has been deliberately evaded. And only in serious cases could money be recovered over a longer period as long as 20 years.
Sentencing decisions are always a matter for the courts.

Suggesting accommodation providers could be jailed for anything less is simply wrong – that is the last resort. The strategic authorities introducing the levy will focus on helping providers get it right.

title: One year as Commissioner for the Tenant Farming Sector

content.content: In September 2025, I took on the role of Commissioner for the Tenant Farming Sector because I believe a thriving tenant farming sector is essential to the future of English agriculture.

Over the past year, my office has brought tenants, landlords and advisers together through regional roundtables. We launched our first sector survey and shared key insights with sector stakeholders and Defra policy colleagues. These conversations and findings have helped us better understand the challenges people face and the importance of raising concerns before relationships break down.

In this post, I’ll explain how we support the whole tenant farming sector, what we’ve heard and how it informs policy. I’ll also share why early contact matters, and our priorities for the next 12 months.
Supporting the whole tenant farming sector

The role was created as recommended in Baroness Rock’s review of the tenant farming sector. The Commissioner’s purpose is to encourage fair working relationships across the tenanted sector, guided by the Agricultural Landlord and Tenant Code of Practice for England, which I’ll refer to as the Code.
One point I have been keen to emphasise since my appointment is that my role covers the whole tenant farming sector, not just tenants.
That distinction matters.

Good tenancy relationships depend on everyone involved working constructively together, including tenants, landlords, agents and solicitors. My office helps encourage constructive conversations and relationships.
Listening is central to this role, and I have been encouraged by how willing people have been to share their experiences.
By listening during our casework, engagements and conversations, we have gained a deeper understanding of the challenges facing tenants, landlords and advisers across the sector.
Several consistent themes have emerged from these conversations including:

With more farmers taking part in Sustainable Farming Incentive and Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier agreements, Landscape Recovery projects, biodiversity initiatives and emerging private markets for nature, people want to understand how tenants can take part fairly and how benefits and responsibilities are shared.

These are often complex issues with no simple answers. Open and constructive dialogue between all parties helps us understand the detail of each issue and identify insights that my team can share anonymously with relevant colleagues in Defra and delivery bodies to inform future policy design.
Helping your experiences shape policy

Turning what we hear into evidence for policy is an important part of our work alongside investigations. Much of this takes place behind the scenes, helping to strengthen understanding of tenant farming issues in wider policy discussions.

We have worked closely with Defra policy colleagues, sharing insights from the sector and contributing evidence through the joint Defra and industry-led ‘Farm Tenancy Forum’. This helps ensure the lived experiences of those involved in agricultural tenancies are better understood by policymakers.

We also launched our first anonymous survey of the tenant farming sector. The results show respondents’ views on relationships, their experiences and their awareness of the Commissioner and the Code. They’ve helped us identify areas for future work.
We shared our findings with representative bodies to highlight the sentiment and challenges reported. We’ll use these results as a starting point to assess our progress in future years.

Our regional roundtables have brought people from across the sector together to discuss common challenges and opportunities. The most recent, in Cornwall, showed the value of creating space for frank, constructive conversations. These discussions can reveal insights formal consultations could miss.
My team and I have also attended industry conferences, agricultural shows, representative body meetings and other events across the country. In the last 6 months, we have:
Our regular regional roundtables have been among the most effective ways to bring people together.
Why raising concerns early matters
One of the clearest lessons from our first year is the value of raising concerns early.

Investigating individual cases of relationship or contractual problems is a major part of our work. Each case is different, but together they help us identify recurring concerns and build a broader picture of the issues affecting the sector.

In a significant number of cases, people contact us only after relationships have broken down or legal proceedings, arbitration or notices to quit are already underway. By then, options become limited, positions become harder to change, trust more difficult to rebuild, and solutions more costly for all parties.

My advice is simple: do not wait until a disagreement becomes a crisis. Raising concerns with my office early gives us more opportunity to identify constructive solutions that may work for both sides.
Even if you are not sure you have a formal case, my office is available to everyone in the sector to raise questions and concerns.
You can contact us through the GOV.UK service or via our mailbox at ctfs@defra.gov.uk.
Looking ahead

Thank you to everyone who has spoken with us, responded to our survey, attended an event or shared experiences, ideas and concerns. I’m also grateful to colleagues across Defra and the wider policy community who have helped establish and develop the office.

There is still much to do. Over the next year, we’ll focus on strengthening the evidence available to the sector. By sharing lessons, case studies and examples of good practice, alongside positive and negative experiences, we want to help people understand what good tenancy relationships look like and how to achieve better outcomes.

We’ll continue to raise awareness of the Commissioner and the Code through more regional roundtables and new ways of sharing our work and findings. A follow-up survey will help us understand what difference our first year’s work has made.

We also want to keep hearing from people across England. We welcome invitations to visit farms and organisations’ offices or join meetings online. These conversations help strengthen collaboration and identify emerging issues early.

I remain committed to supporting a thriving, professional and resilient tenant farming sector. That means promoting the Code, encouraging open discussion and helping people build stronger working relationships.

The sector faces considerable challenges, but it also has significant opportunities through food production, environmental work and its contribution to rural economies. Working together will help tenants, landlords and advisers make the most of those opportunities.

title: Prepare for gear changes

content.content: The UK and EU have agreed a package of additional technical fisheries measures for 2026 to support the recovery of severely depleted fish stocks in the Celtic Sea, Channel and Irish Sea.
These measures respond to scientific advice indicating critical stock conditions, including zero-catch advice for certain Celtic Sea cod, haddock and whiting stocks.
The agreed approach focuses on increasing fishing gear selectivity, particularly through larger mesh sizes and mandatory use of selective devices designed to reduce the capture of vulnerable species.

The measures apply primarily to vessels using otter trawls, seines and beam trawls and are intended to reduce bycatch of cod, haddock, whiting, sole and plaice while allowing sustainable fishing opportunities for other target species such as anglerfish, hake, megrim and nephrops.
The measures

Fishing vessels operating in the designated Celtic Sea Protection Zone will be required to use larger cod-end mesh sizes in trawl nets or install more selective escape panels and sorting devices that allow juvenile and vulnerable fish to escape.

The measures are intended to reduce unwanted catches of cod, haddock and whiting while maintaining fishing opportunities for species such as monkfish (anglerfish), hake, megrim and nephrops, better known as Dublin Bay prawns or langoustines.

Vessels targeting nephrops will face some of the most significant changes. Boats with catches containing more than 30% Norway lobster will be required to fit specialist selective equipment such as Nordmøre sorting grids, Netgrid devices or large-mesh escape panels designed to prevent cod and other depleted species from entering the catch.
Channel Fisheries Face New Restrictions

The agreement also introduces tougher measures in the English Channel, where stocks of cod, sole and plaice are considered depleted. Vessels using trawls and seines in ICES Division 7e will generally be required to use 100mm cod-end mesh sizes. Fisheries previously operating with smaller meshes will be required to increase to at least 90mm subject to permitted derogations, a move expected to reduce the capture of younger fish and allow more individuals to reach spawning age.
Officials have also committed to considering further restrictions in the eastern Channel during 2026, including the possibility of increasing minimum mesh sizes for additional trawl fisheries.
Irish Sea Measures Target Cod and Whiting Recovery
In the Irish Sea, attention is focused on rebuilding cod and whiting stocks, both of which remain at historically low levels.

Nephrops fisheries will again be required to adopt additional selective gear aimed at reducing bycatch of these species. Catch thresholds will be monitored using the live weight of fish landed after each trip.
Recovery Plans to Follow
The UK and EU have also committed to ongoing scientific monitoring and technical reviews.

Officials have been working on longer-term rebuilding plans for the most vulnerable stocks, with the aim of restoring populations to levels capable of delivering Maximum Sustainable Yield, the internationally recognised benchmark for sustainable fisheries management.
These changes were subject to licence conditions made on 1 November and will become enforceable on 26 November 2026.

title: Protecting England's seahorses, stalked jellyfish and the seagrass meadows they depend on

content.content: England’s seas support some of our most important and sensitive marine habitats and species, many of which are protected within marine protected areas (MPAs).
This includes seagrass, an important habitat for some of our most fascinating marine species, the seahorse and the stalked jellyfish.
Both depend on seagrass a marine flowering plant, which forms underwater meadows within the shelter of shallow, protected bays.

Understanding how marine non-licensable activities (mNLA) interact with seagrass and the species it supports is essential for informing future management decisions in MPAs and helping to protect them for future generations.
Seahorses
One of our most intriguing marine species associated with seagrass meadows is the seahorse.

Seahorses wrap their tails around seagrass to anchor themselves while feeding, sheltering and breeding. England's waters support two species of seahorse, the spiny. or long snouted seahorse (Hippocampus guttulatus) and the short snouted seahorse (Hippocampus hippocampus). Both species are protected under UK wildlife legislation.
Stalked jellyfish
Another less well known but nationally important species that can be found in seagrass beds and other shallow-water habitats in the UK, is the stalked jellyfish.

Not all jellyfish drift with the ocean currents, and unlike the free-swimming jellyfish most people are familiar with, stalked jellyfish are found attached to vegetation or algae and spend much of their lives fixed in one place, stalked jellyfish are rare and have specialised habitat requirements.
The UK is home to a number of species including the St. John’s stalked jellyfish (Calvadosia cruxmelitensis) and the kaleidoscope jellyfish (Haliclystus octoradiatus).
The value of seagrass

In the UK, we have two species of seagrass, the common eelgrass (Zostera marina) and dwarf eelgrass (Zostera noltii). Seagrass beds are among the most valuable coastal habitats in the UK as they stabilise sediment, improve water quality, store carbon, provide nursery areas for commercially important fish species and support a wide range of marine life.

Seagrass is gaining global recognition for its environmental importance, with Blue Planet III showcasing how these underwater meadows help sustain life on Earth by generating oxygen and supporting marine biodiversity.
Impacts of marine recreation

Seagrass habitats are vulnerable to physical disturbance because their roots and rhizomes lie close to the seabed surface. Anchoring, in particular, has been found to have a significant impact on this habitat. Anchors and anchor chains can disturb, uproot and damage seagrass plants during deployment, while vessels swing at anchor and during anchor retrieval. Repeated anchoring can create bare patches known as anchor scars, fragmenting seagrass beds and reducing their ability to recover.

Healthy seagrass habitats are essential for supporting seahorse and stalked jellyfish populations. Damage to these habitats can therefore have knock-on effects for the species that rely on them. Fragmentation and habitat loss can affect the distribution and survival of both species by reducing suitable attachment surfaces for stalked jellyfish, and the feeding opportunities, shelter and breeding habitat available to seahorses.
Recovery through management

Evidence from Studland Bay Marine Conservation Zone has shown encouraging signs of seagrass recovery following the introduction of a voluntary no anchor zone and the installation and use of advanced mooring systems also known as eco-moorings. Monitoring has identified new areas of seagrass growth and reductions in the size of previously recorded anchor scars. Learn more: Studland Bay seagrass shows dramatic recovery as MMO backed eco-moorings prove effective.
These findings demonstrate how targeted, evidence-led management measures can support habitat recovery while allowing people to continue enjoying the marine environment responsibly.
Have your say

MMO is currently seeking additional evidence on the impacts of mNLA on birds, benthic habitats, reef, and seagrass. If you have relevant research, monitoring data, reports or observations, we ask you to respond to our current call for evidence and respond before it closes on 25 November 2026.
By sharing information, you can help improve our understanding of these impacts and support the effective protection of England’s seagrass beds and associated species that rely on them.

For more detailed guidance on how to contribute, why this is important and the types of evidence that we find useful, please visit our previous blog: Share your evidence on the impacts of recreational activities in England’s marine protected areas (MPAs) – Marine Development Blog
If you require support completing our survey or submitting evidence, please let us know: conservation@marinemanagement.org.uk

title: Enhancing public protection and helping probation staff focus on what matters most

content.content: Probation staff play a vital role in supervising people released into the community, managing risk and protecting the public. They work closely with people on probation to support compliance with licence conditions and reduce the potential for reoffending. For some offenders, this includes wearing an electronic monitoring tag, which can provide location information to support supervision and risk management.
Introducing our new Electronic Monitoring Data Insights (EMDI) tool

As demand on probation services continues to grow, giving our practitioners timely access to monitoring information is increasingly important. As part of our work to modernise our services, our new EMDI tool is helping staff obtain and use GPS tagging information more efficiently.
Turning data into operational insight

EMDI provides faster access to key location and behavioural data through our digital systems, reducing the need for time-consuming manual processes. The tool brings together information from across electronic monitoring services into a single, intuitive platform, helping our practitioners quickly understand offender movement patterns, assess compliance and take appropriate and proportionate action where necessary.
By making monitoring information easier to access and interpret, EMDI supports frontline staff to make timely, evidence-informed decisions when managing people on probation.
Delivering measurable benefits

The tool is currently being piloted across our London, West Midlands and East of England probation regions, with thousands of users already carrying out over 30,000 searches. Early feedback has been extremely positive, with testing indicating the tool saves an average of 21 minutes per week for every person on probation whose trail monitoring data is reviewed.
Described as a “game changer” the tool is already delivering tangible benefits for probation staff:
Looking ahead

We will continue to monitor usage, learn from feedback and look for new opportunities to maximise the capability of EMDI; ensuring the service continues to evolve in line with the needs of probation staff.

Our ambition is to roll-out EDMI across all probation regions by the end of 2026; enabling our practitioners to respond more effectively to emerging risks, while spending more time supporting people on probation to achieve positive outcomes.

EMDI is just one of a growing suite of innovations helping to stabilise and transform our electronic monitoring services; equipping frontline staff with the tools they need to reduce reoffending, protect victims and keep the public safe.

title: One year of accelerators, in their own words
authors: Anna Goss, Deputy Director - Test, Learn and Grow, Public Sector Reform, Cabinet Office

content.content: A year ago the Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) programme launched our first accelerator projects. Last month we marked that anniversary with an event bringing the whole programme together and the launch of our new TLG Playbook, informed and shaped by the on the ground learning from our accelerators over the past year.

Rather than tell the story ourselves, we asked each accelerator team to share in their own words what they set out to do, a moment from the year that's stuck with them, and what they're carrying forward.
Northumberland and Manchester: integrated family support
Lesley Grieve, Test, Learn and Grow Project Lead at Northumberland County Council

We launched our accelerator in autumn 2025 to help meet one of the Government's top priorities, getting 75% of children to a Good Level of Development by 2028. Family Hubs had a central role to play, but good support was not always reaching the families who needed it most.

Rather than designing a solution centrally, we started by listening to parents, frontline workers and local partners to meet them in places where they were. In Northumberland, one idea rose to the top: short "Ready to Learn" sessions for two-year-olds, delivered in schools by Family Hub staff. We set out to test how we identify families, how we invite them, and how we deliver sessions.

Going back to parents directly changed everything. They wanted trusted messengers, not official channels, and flexible sessions, not a long programme. They cared about their immediate struggles at home like behaviour and potty training, not generic content. And sometimes their biggest stress wasn't development at all, it was not knowing school application deadlines or how to apply for nursery funding. Starting small and really understanding the needs of families meant our failures were cheap, saving an estimated £35,000 in staff costs, and meant we built something with parents, not for them.
Wakefield: economic inactivity
Sharon Marshall, Employment Strategy Manager at Step-Up (Wakefield Council’s in-house employment service)

More than a million young people aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training. While the Get Britain Working White Paper sets out the government's wider ambition to tackle this, and Milburn’s Review is investigating the root causes, the Wakefield accelerator set out to test what actually works.

Working as a blended team, TLG colleagues reset how local and central government work together, and let young people's own experiences set the direction, rather than consultation alone. TLG colleagues fitted into the local offices really well with other colleagues asking “Who are that team?” and “Aren’t they really good?” which has challenged a lot of people’s perception of what a Cabinet Office civil servant looks like.
Our focus is now testing how work experience can work better for both employers and young people, and how to give more holistic support that meets them where they are.

From the outset, the team's genuine enthusiasm for making real changes to reduce and prevent youth unemployment in Wakefield has been clear. After 40 years in local government, working as part of a blended team with TLG colleagues has put the fire back in my belly.
Barnsley and Essex: AI and data support to the frontline
Nicky Arnold, Senior Service Designer, Test, Learn and Grow, Cabinet Office

This accelerator set out to explore how data and AI could support a shift toward prevention in children's services, so families get the right support at the right time. We worked with Barnsley Children's Services to map the system we were testing in.

Our service designer spent time in Barnsley having conversations with these professions with social work experience, which started as technical and process-driven became something deeper. Social workers shared stories of children and families that had stayed with them, and the difficulties of advocating for them, giving our team an in-depth understanding of the real challenges people face in this complex area. Building that trust, before anything else, turned out to be the work itself, not a step before it. We carry that into year two as we find our place in the overlap between test and learn, AI, and children's services.
Liverpool and Plymouth: neighbourhood health
Josh Lowe, Senior Service Designer, Test, Learn and Grow, Cabinet Office

Have you, or someone you love, ever had a serious health problem? Sometimes, severe conditions are sadly unavoidable. But most of us know people who could have escaped a terrible experience if the right support had been accessible nearby, or if different professionals had brought their insight together at the right time. This is what the government’s Neighbourhood Health agenda - and our accelerator - hopes to tackle: how to make sure healthy lives are created and sustained in the places people live, meaning fewer of us have to rely on intensive services like hospital care.

There are so many moments of joy - and moments of frustration - that stick with us from our work with our brilliant partners in Liverpool and Plymouth. But one is our first visit to the SWAGGA Primary Care Network, one of our operational partners in delivering a preventative respiratory healthcare test in South Liverpool. A banner in the lobby of one of their neighbourhood hubs reads: “We don’t look for reasons why something can’t be done. We look for solutions that make it possible.”

That sentiment sums up the work of so many amazing professionals in Liverpool, Plymouth, and elsewhere, often working against the system to bring together the right professionals in the right places to meet people’s needs. Our mission for the next year and beyond is to explore how the system might start to shift to working with them, so that joined-up, preventative and person centred care becomes routine, not the exception.
Sandwell and Nottingham: SEND employment transitions
Lauren Abraham, Senior Service Designer, Test, Learn and Grow, Cabinet Office

When young people with SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) leave education, their support, relationships and structures around them can disappear overnight. For too many people this leads to poor employment, health and independence outcomes, which are costly to reverse and hard on the young people and families involved.

The Government set out ambitious SEND reforms in the Schools White Paper. The TLG SEND accelerator partnered with Sandwell and Nottingham to test, in real places, with real young people, how reforms might actually work for the young people and families living it.

The moment that stuck with us came early. We ran two co-design workshops with young people with SEND at Sandwell College, deliberately spaced apart so they'd get to know us before the second, deeper conversation. They mapped their own journeys, the people who'd helped them, and what good support should look and feel like. They were generous with experiences that weren't always easy to share, and what they told us is already reshaping how we think about identifying young people before things go wrong. That's carried through everything since, listening first, designing second.
Islington: Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG)
Aisling Barker, VAWG Operational Adviser, Test, Learn and Grow, Cabinet Office

When the UK’s VAWG strategy was launched in December 2025, the pledge to halve VAWG in 10 years remained an ambitious and welcome goal.  But how can test and learn ways of working help? This is a broad goal that required the accelerator team in Islington to narrow down to find a starting point to test.
We launched in Islington in January 2026 and spent five months speaking to frontline practitioners and, crucially, to survivors of domestic abuse about what should change.

Our workshops surfaced many ideas and themes. The need to support children experiencing domestic abuse at home was a theme that came out of our research, and Islington felt it connected with their own strategy. We learned that our job was not to pick the best one, but to break it down into something small enough to test safely and low-cost.

We are now testing ways to bring support to children affected by domestic abuse who are not in contact with statutory services, working alongside practitioners, who know this work inside and out, and carry the voices of survivors with them every day, and survivors themselves through Islington Voices for Change.

That's six places, ten teams, and many different versions of the same lesson: start small, listen hard, and let what you learn change what you do next. There are more stories like these across the programme, so follow the blog to stay updated. And if you want to get more involved in testing, learning and growing with us, join the TLG Network.

description: Our accelerator teams share in their own words insights from their work over the past year and tell us about some of their highlights along the way.

title: Getting out of the building: Learning from our colleagues

content.content: Do you really understand how your products are used in context?

One challenge I've observed while working across policy, operations and delivery teams is that we often think of ourselves as separate groups with different objectives. Policy teams can sometimes see delivery teams as the people who implement policy, while delivery teams can view policy teams as their customers. In reality, neither is true. We are all working towards the same outcome and each team brings a different perspective that is essential to designing effective services.

The difficulty is that even though we are all working towards the same goal, we operate in different contexts. How well do you understand how people use your service, and what might you be missing if you do not see their work yourself?
This is where one of the most important principles of product management comes in: "getting out of the building."

Put simply, if we are designing and delivering digital services for people, we need to spend time understanding how those people actually work. Insights from user research and data are essential, but there is no substitute for also sitting alongside users, observing their day-to-day reality.
Getting out of my building

Last month I got out of my building in Wigan to visit London-based colleagues in the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI). OTSI colleagues, and the businesses they serve, are the primary users of services designed and delivered by the Digital, Data and Technology team I am part of. Close collaboration between the 2 teams helps ensure digital products support the realities of sanctions casework. It is essential that we understand the operational environment in which those services are used.

Before visiting OTSI, much of my casework understanding came from conversations with managers, workshops and requirements discussions. These are all valuable sources of information, but they inevitably provide a higher-level view of how work happens. I believed we would be better equipped to make decisions about systems and services that directly affect caseworkers if we had a deeper understanding of their day-to-day work.

The purpose of the visit was straightforward: to spend time with OTSI caseworkers to understand how they do their jobs, the complexity of their work, and the everyday challenges they encounter. I wanted to understand how caseworkers manage cases, identify pain points, and uncover opportunities to improve the tools and processes they use.

I was fortunate to visit on a day when a team leader was inducting a new caseworker. This provided a particularly useful opportunity to see how experienced staff work through cases, and how new colleagues are introduced to the service, its processes, systems and terminology.
Seeing the work first-hand helped me build empathy for caseworkers and begin to bridge the gap between how we think work happens and how it actually happens in practice.
Making our products work for users

As product professionals, one of our responsibilities is to identify opportunities for improvement and ensure they are reflected in future planning and prioritisation. The session highlighted several areas where we may be able to improve the user experience over time. Some opportunities were relatively small, such as simplifying naming conventions and terminology. We learned that using simpler and more consistent language could help reduce cognitive load for both new and experienced users. We also identified opportunities to use existing DDaT capabilities to streamline processes, rather than creating entirely new solutions.
These observations do not currently represent a finished solution, and they will need to be considered alongside other priorities. However, they demonstrate the value of seeing users at work.

Spending time with caseworkers surfaced specific opportunities that can now inform future product decisions. The insights have been captured and will be considered for future prioritisation alongside evolving business needs.

What struck me most was the complexity of the work caseworkers undertake. It was important to understand not just the technology they use, but the wider context in which they operate. When developing products and services, it can be easy to focus on features, requirements and delivery milestones.

Spending time with users provides a valuable reminder that every feature we build sits within a much larger operational process. Seeing how people make decisions, where they spend most of their time, and where frustrations occur allows us to make better product decisions and ultimately deliver greater value.
Getting out of the building is not just for product teams

Although 'getting out of the building' is often associated with product management, its value extends far beyond product teams. Whether you're a developer, business analyst, delivery manager, user researcher, interaction designer, architect or tester, spending time with the people who use our services can provide insights that cannot be captured in a backlog item or meeting note. By observing real users in their working environment, we develop a deeper understanding of the problems we are trying to solve and build stronger relationships with the teams we support.

My visit to OTSI reinforced just how valuable these interactions can be. It gave me a much better understanding of what matters most to caseworkers, how the service operates in practice, and where future opportunities may exist to improve the experience.
Ensuring the visit counts
The immediate next step is to reconnect with the team, clarify several follow-up questions that emerged from the session, and continue building our understanding of the caseworker experience.

The experience has encouraged me to build more of this engagement into my approach to product management. By spending time with a wider range of operational teams and users, I hope to develop a deeper understanding of their challenges and test assumptions earlier. This will ensure that future improvements are grounded in the realities of day-to-day work.
Building better solutions
Getting out of the building is ultimately about working together. If you work in Digital, Data and Technology, spend time with the people who use your services.
If you work in policy or operations, give your digital colleagues the opportunity to sit alongside your users and understand their work.
Bring us in. Let us understand the problem together, and together we can build better solutions.

title: Human health: the UK's hidden economic cost of climate change

content.content: When people think about the economic costs of climate change, they often picture flooded homes, damaged infrastructure or disaster recovery. Yet some of the most significant costs may arise through a less visible pathway: human health.

Climate-related hazards, including extreme heat, flooding and storms, can affect physical and mental health. So much so that the UK Health Security Agency identifies climate change as a growing public health risk in the UK.

To help policymakers understand and incorporate these risks into decision-making, GAD has recently supported a range of climate and health-related projects. These aim to improve understanding of how climate-related changes in population health may affect:
This includes systems mapping and quantitative modelling to help policymakers explore long-term risks and potential policy responses.

Climate driven health impacts have implications for workforce participation, productivity, healthcare demand and public finances. Unlike damage to buildings or infrastructure, however, many of these effects are not immediately visible and can be difficult to quantify. One way to think about the economic consequences of climate-related hazards is as an iceberg. While damage to infrastructure and property is often visible, many wider costs emerge indirectly, including through impacts on population health.
Figure 1 provides a simplified illustration of how some climate-related economic impacts may be more visible than others.
Health and economic performance

Population health is an important determinant of economic performance. It affects people’s ability to work, their productivity and their use of public services. Even before considering climate change, ill health creates significant economic and fiscal pressures. For example:
These figures illustrate the scale of existing health-related challenges.

Allowing for the effects of climate change may impact these costs substantially. Analysis by the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics estimates that climate-related mortality could reduce UK gross domestic product (GDP) by around 0.4% on average over the end-of-century period (2081-2100). This estimate is based on a current policies scenario, which assumes existing global climate commitments are implemented but no additional mitigation action is taken.

However, mortality represents only one aspect of climate-related health impacts, and the estimate does not capture wider effects such as ill health, pressures on healthcare services or productivity losses.
Climate change and population health

Climate change may affect not only mortality, but also the number of years people spend in good health. Measures such as healthy life expectancy can help us understand these wider impacts and their implications for individuals, public services and the economy. This is discussed further in GAD's blog, Not all years lived are equal: understanding measures of health.
Over time, some risks associated with extreme cold may decline, and climate mitigation and adaptation can generate important additional health benefits.

Actions to mitigate climate change can also generate health benefits, for example through improvements in air quality that may reduce some respiratory illnesses. However, risks associated with extreme heat and other climate-related hazards are expected to increase. The scale, timing and overall consequences of future impacts remain uncertain and will depend on factors such as:

If climate change adversely affects population health, it could compound existing challenges such as population ageing and stalling healthy life expectancy. These impacts are unlikely to be distributed evenly, with some groups potentially facing greater health risks and having fewer opportunities to adapt, contributing to wider social inequalities. This would further increase pressures on labour markets, welfare spending and public services.
The health-related economic burden

Climate-related health impacts do not affect the economy through a single route. They can influence labour markets, public services and public finances through multiple interconnected pathways. These effects may reinforce one another through feedback loops, making the overall impact difficult to assess in isolation. While simplified, the graphic below illustrates some of these potential pathways.
Connecting climate, health and economic policy

Although some climate-related health effects may be reflected in GDP, the measure alone does not capture their full impact on wellbeing or public finances. For example, higher healthcare spending may increase measured economic activity while also reflecting worsening health outcomes and greater demands on public resources.

Existing tools such as the Office for Budget Responsibility’s Fiscal Risks and Sustainability reports and HM Treasury's Green Book already support long-term risk assessment and policy appraisal. As evidence develops, climate-related health impacts could be considered more explicitly, helping provide a fuller picture of long-term risks.
Making the hidden costs more visible
GAD has recently explored these issues through a range of climate and health-related projects, including:
These projects illustrate how GAD’s support is helping policymakers understand and respond to the wider economic consequences of climate-related health impacts.
Looking ahead

As climate risks intensify, understanding their implications for population health may become increasingly important. These impacts are relevant not only to public health policy, but also to decisions affecting labour markets, welfare systems and the long-term sustainability of government finances.

GAD operates at the intersection of government policy, long-term financial sustainability, uncertainty and analytical assurance. We combine actuarial analysis with expertise in climate science and work closely with specialists in areas such as public health and economics. By bringing these perspectives together, we can help make the hidden health-related costs of climate change more visible, supporting better-informed government decisions.

title: What is a support-first approach to school attendance?

content.content: Support starts with understanding why
Going to school regularly helps children learn, spend time with friends and be part of their school community. That is why children should be in school every day they can.
When a child is struggling to come in, the starting point – for both you as a parent and the school – should be understanding why.
Your child’s school should listen, understand and work with you to overcome challenges.
What does a support-first approach mean?

Schools should take a supportive approach to helping your child to regularly attend school. A support-first approach means understanding why a child might be finding it difficult to go to school and working together with the family to address those barriers.
Schools should listen to the child and their parents, agree practical support, and review whether it is helping.
What support can families expect from their school?
Support should reflect your child’s age, needs and circumstances. Schools should:
Listen to you and your child
Explore what is making coming to school difficult, including worries at school or pressures at home.
Agree practical steps together
For a primary-aged child, this might involve support with morning routines, separation or transitions. For a secondary-aged child, it might focus on friendships, particular lessons, exams or travel.
Make support personal

Children with physical or mental health conditions or special educational needs and disabilities may need additional support or reasonable adjustments. Plans should be agreed with the family and reviewed.
Bring in other help where needed
Schools may work with the local authority, health, mental health, SEND, early help or other local services if needed such as a local family hub.
Start the conversation early
Problems can become harder to address once patterns are established.
What can parents do?
As a parent or carer, you have an important role in supporting your child go to school everyday.
Talk to your child and their school if you spot any changes in behaviour, difficulties in the morning or circumstances at home that may be affecting them.
You do not need to know the solution before asking for help. School will work together with you to agree manageable steps, then review what is and is not working.
A useful approach for one child may not suit another, and support may need to change as children grow or their circumstances change.

You can also make sure you are familiar with the NHS ‘is my child to ill for school’ advice and where possible book medical appointments outside of school time. If that's not possible, send them in before and after the appointment so they don’t miss a full day.

It’s also important to recognise that children with long-term medical conditions, serious mental health challenges, or special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) may encounter additional obstacles. For those experiencing complex barriers to attendance, schools should engage in compassionate discussions with both children and their families, collaborating to provide tailored support that meets their specific needs.

title: Beyond the floodwater: the lasting impact of flooding and coastal change
authors: Julie Foley, Director of Flood Risk Strategy & Adaptation at the Environment Agency

content.content: When we think about flooding and coastal erosion, it is often the physical impacts that come to mind: flooded homes, damaged businesses, disrupted infrastructure and changing coastlines.

However, the effects can go much further. Flooding can affect people’s mental health and wellbeing, finances and sense of security, with impacts that can continue long after the flood water has gone. Coastal erosion can create uncertainty about the future of places people know and value.

Two recent Environment Agency research projects are helping us better understand these wider impacts. One looks at how people experience and recover from flooding. The other explores what we know about the relationship between coastal erosion and mental health.
Together, they show why understanding people’s experiences is an important part of managing flood and coastal change risk.
Supporting communities after flooding
Recovery from flooding does not end when the immediate emergency is over.

Our research project, Understanding and supporting the flood recovery process, found that recovery can continue for months or even years. People may be dealing with repairs, insurance claims and grants, replacing possessions, rebuilding routines and adapting to the possibility of future flooding.

The research reviewed more than 100 sources of evidence and included interviews with national stakeholders and case studies involving residents, businesses and local organisations in Bewdley, Looe, Sparkhill and Stockdalewath.

Recovery is different for everyone. People’s experiences can be shaped by their income, previous experience of flooding, community networks and access to support. Low-income households, tenants, rural communities and some minority communities face additional barriers to recovery and accessing support.
Local relationships can make a significant difference. Neighbours, voluntary organisations and community groups provide practical help, emotional support and trusted information.

The research identified examples of effective recovery, including strong multi-agency coordination, rapid activation of recovery arrangements, affordable insurance through Flood Re and greater uptake of property flood resilience measures through Build Back Better.

But there remain challenges. People can struggle to navigate insurance and grant processes, receive inconsistent information or find that support ends before their recovery is complete. For some, the mental health impacts of flooding continue long after physical repairs have been completed.

The research highlights the importance of authorities staying visible, communicating clearly and working with partners and communities throughout recovery. It shows that recovery is about helping people, communities and local economies both recover and become more resilient to future flooding.
Understanding mental health and coastal erosion

Our research project, Valuing the Mental Health Costs of Coastal Erosion, explored what is known about how living with coastal erosion risk may affect mental health and wellbeing. The study combined a review of existing research, analysis of national datasets from England and Wales, and interviews with practitioners.

One of the key themes was uncertainty. People living in areas at risk of coastal erosion may face years of uncertainty about what will happen to their homes and communities, sometimes before any physical loss of coastline occurs.

The literature review identified examples of stress, anxiety and other negative impacts on wellbeing associated with coastal erosion. Practitioners also highlighted concerns about housing, finances, displacement and the potential loss of people’s connection to where they live.

Although the research identified evidence of mental health and wellbeing concerns associated with coastal erosion, the available national datasets did not allow us to fully quantify these impacts. Further work is needed to understand how people experience the uncertainty and change associated with a changing coastline.

Through the Coastal Adaptation Pilots, we are testing practical approaches to help communities prepare for and adapt to long-term coastal change. These pilots will help us build our understanding of the real-world mental health impacts on communities living with coastal erosion risk.
Putting people at the heart of resilience
The evidence demonstrates why people’s experiences need to remain at the heart of flood and coastal change risk management.

As the challenges associated with flooding and coastal change continue to grow, this evidence will help shape future research, policy and practice. Most importantly, it will help ensure that people’s needs, experiences and wellbeing remain central to how we plan, adapt and build resilience for the future.
