title: Supporting fairer agricultural supply chains: our second annual report

content.content: When I became Agricultural Supply Chain Adjudicator (ASCA), I knew regulations alone would not make contracts between producers and processors fairer. Of course, the rules are vitally important, but people also need to feel confident using them.
Producers need to know their rights, processors need to understand their responsibilities, and everyone needs to know that concerns can be raised safely and will be taken seriously.

My second annual report outlines my office’s work with the dairy and pig sectors during my second year in the role - including the handling of formal and informal enquiries. It covers our engagement with the sectors, and the intelligence we've gathered to help shape policy.

In this post, I share highlights from that work, explain how we have helped resolve contractual concerns and outline our priorities for the year ahead. I also explain how you can contact my team for advice or raise a concern in confidence.
Our work with the dairy and pig sectors
Over the past year, producers and processors across the dairy and pig sectors have told me how changing market conditions are affecting their businesses. In summary:
Against this backdrop, my team has focused on helping producers and processors understand their obligations and manage contractual concerns.

With the Fair Dealing Obligations (Milk) Regulations 2024 (FDOM24) fully in force for over a year now, we have focused on how they work in practice. The regulations provide important protections, but understanding how they apply remains a challenge. Some producers fear that raising concerns could damage commercial relationships. My team monitors these issues and uses what we hear to identify emerging concerns, engage with producers and processors, and encourage more open and effective communication across the supply chain.

The Fair Dealing Obligations (Pigs) Regulations 2025 (FDOP) came into force for new contracts on 13 August 2025, with the transition period for existing contracts ending on 13 August 2026. Prior to full implementation, we focused on building awareness and getting to know the sector. We have worked with producers and processors to gather evidence about current practice and identify practical information to help them adapt to the requirements.

My team has engaged widely with producers, processors and representative bodies across the dairy and pig sectors through online and in-person meetings, sector events, farm and processor visits, agricultural shows and roundtables.

Concerns raised at an agricultural show led to a processor amending its contract to address a producer’s concerns and ensure compliance. Our roundtables brought farming unions, processors and representative bodies together to identify shared concerns, encourage better communication and transparency, and explore industry-led codes of practice.

Drawing on our casework, confidential reporting and wider engagement, we also gave evidence to the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee inquiry into fairness in the supply chain, highlighting contractual fairness, market transparency and barriers to raising complaints.

These conversations have helped people understand and apply the regulations and raise confidential queries and concerns, including formal complaints. They have also helped us understand how contracts work in practice.
Clearer contracts & effective communication
One message has come through clearly this year: good relationships are easier when contracts are clear and communication is timely and effective.

Written contracts, transparent pricing and straightforward processes for making changes all help reduce uncertainty. They can also make it easier to have the right conversations early, before problems become disputes.

In meetings, at events and in direct conversations, I have heard how useful it is when clear, transparent information is shared effectively and in a timely way. We have seen good examples of this where processors provide their producers with insight and rationale to what's happening in the wider sector.
Unfortunately, we have also seen examples where changes are poorly communicated and implemented, so it's understandable when some producers get frustrated and turn to ASCA for advice.
Resolving informal disputes in practice
The latest annual report includes case studies which highlight the work our office undertakes to resolve disputes before they intensify:

A focus of our office over the next year will be to build more of these case studies, both in the milk and pig sectors. Our hope is that they highlight the benefits of early communication with the ASCA office and help build understanding and awareness of how both FDOM24 and FDOP operate in practice.
How to raise concerns with the ASCA
I understand that some producers may feel apprehensive about raising a concern with my office, especially if they are worried it might impact on important commercial relationships.

I encourage anyone experiencing uncertainty or concern with their contractual arrangements to get in touch with my office as early as possible. In many cases, engaging my office as soon as issues become apparent can help to amicably resolve issues before they escalate.

If you have a concern about your contractual relationship or want to understand whether an issue may be covered by the regulations, you can contact my team before making a formal complaint. You can raise concerns informally or through our in-confidence service, including anonymously. You do not need to have a fully formed complaint before speaking to us.
Farming unions or other representatives can also approach us on your behalf.

Our approach is centred on early, proportionate and good-faith engagement. We will listen to the concerns raised and, where appropriate, seek to engage constructively with those involved before reaching conclusions. As the case studies demonstrate, acting as an impartial intermediary can help both sides understand the issues, improve communication and find practical solutions before problems become more entrenched.

The important thing is to talk to us. Whether you are looking for initial advice, want to raise something in confidence or simply are not sure whether an issue falls within our remit, my team is here to listen and help identify the most appropriate way forward.
Find out how to contact the ASCA and which route to use.
Next steps for the ASCA

Over the next year, my team will keep building trust across the industry by meeting producers and processors, providing practical advice and delivering consistent support. We will listen to all parts of the sectors we cover to help focus our work where it can make the most difference.

My office has already started working with the egg sector. As fair dealing regulations are developed for other agricultural sectors, our role is likely to expand. I want us to use our experience with milk and pigs to help those sectors put new regulations into practice and, if designated, enforce them.

We will continue bringing industry together to strengthen supply chain relationships and support discussions on industry-led codes of practice. At our dairy roundtable, participants committed to working together on an industry-wide code. Our September 2026 pig roundtable explored the value of a similar code. I want us to help industry develop practical solutions that improve communication, transparency and trust.

I want to make it easier to contact my office by improving our GOV.UK information and explaining the different ways to raise concerns. We will also improve how we use information from producers, representative bodies and others to spot emerging issues and guide our work.
Learn more
To hear more about the issues and activities of the ASCA in the first annual report in 2025, listen to Richard’s Farming Podcast episode on fairer supply chains.
In the episode, Richard is joined by Paul Tompkins, NFU Dairy Board Chair, and Michael Masters, Head of Milk Supply and Operations at Barber’s Farmhouse Cheesemakers.

title: AI in Action: practical AI workshops for local government
authors: Kat Sexton, Deputy Director for Local AI

content.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) is already changing how people work across the public sector. However, making the most of AI is not just about having access to new technology. It is also about having the confidence and practical skills to understand where AI can add value and how it can be used responsibly in day-to-day work.
That is the focus of this year’s annual Civil Service initiative One Big Thing 2026: AI in Action.
What is One Big Thing?
One Big Thing is an annual Civil Service programme that brings civil servants together to focus on a shared area of learning. In 2026, AI in Action is focused on putting AI into practice.

This means helping people identify where AI could be useful, from saving time on everyday tasks to finding simpler ways to get work done. It also aims to build confidence in trying new AI tools and exploring how they could be applied to different tasks and ways of working.
What we are doing for local government

As part of the One Big Thing programme, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) has developed workshop materials for civil servant colleagues across the department, and the Local AI team is making those materials available to local government teams to use, so that they can run those workshops within their own teams.
What do the workshops involve?
The workshops help teams explore how AI could support their own work.
They cover 3 areas:

Workshops can be run within existing teams by team leaders or colleagues with an interest in AI. Facilitators do not need to be AI specialists, and supporting materials and guidance are provided to help them run the sessions.
Why this matters: supporting local government to make the most of AI
Across local government, councils are already exploring how AI can help improve services, support staff and tackle some of the practical challenges they face every day.

Through Local AI, MHCLG is working alongside councils to support the responsible and effective adoption of AI across the sector. Our focus is on helping local government move from interest and experimentation towards practical use, building the confidence, capability and connections needed to apply AI to real problems and deliver better outcomes for communities.

A key part of this is making sure councils can benefit from useful tools, learning and approaches being developed across government, rather than having to solve the same challenges separately. That is why, this year, we are making One Big Thing 2026: AI in Action available to colleagues in local government.
Interested in using the workshop materials?
Local government teams interested in using the AI in Action workshop materials can register by providing their name, organisation and email address through our short form:

Materials will be sent directly to registered contacts for use within their teams.

title: Power of Attorney Stories: Tracey

content.content: [English] - [Cymraeg]

A lasting power of attorney, also known as an LPA, is a legal document. It allows you to nominate someone you trust to step in and make decisions about your health and welfare and property and finance if you lack mental capacity to do so.

Tracey, 45, from Birmingham, was an attorney for her mum and is currently one for her dad, alongside her sister Clare. Here, she shares how being an attorney helped her family through her mum's declining health, and offers her tips for staying organised when acting jointly with a sibling.
“I first came across LPAs years ago, when I worked for a financial advisor. But I didn't really understand what was involved until my own parents decided to set theirs up.

My parents had a property and finance LPA made, and then a health and welfare LPA, which Clare helped them with. They appointed me and my sister Clare jointly and severally for both, meaning we could make decisions together or independently of each other.
Getting started as an attorney

When the LPAs were registered, the first thing I did was add it to the ‘Use an LPA’ service. The service allows donors and attorneys to create an account to give organisations access to view the details of that LPA online.

One thing I'd say to reassure other attorneys is that adding your LPA to the Use service does not put it into action. I used my parents' LPA activation key straight away, but Clare held off for a while, worried that registering it might set things in motion before they were needed. That's simply not the case, it just means everything is ready and waiting for when you do need it.

Once both LPAs were added to the service, using them day to day was straightforward. We were able to see a one-page online summary of the LPAs and create access codes for organisations to view them, which was particularly helpful with bigger organisations like Barclays, British Gas and British Telecom.

We started actively using the finance LPA at the end of last November, as my mum's health began to decline. My dad has full mental capacity, but he'd never dealt with the finances himself, that was always my mum's role. Having the LPA in place meant we could begin a gradual handover, taking on more of the day-to-day management for him. He's never had to speak to a bank or a utility company in his life, and it makes him anxious, so being able to step in on his behalf has genuinely made things easier.
Staying organised with my sister

One thing I'd really encourage other attorneys to consider is setting up shared systems with anyone you're acting alongside. Clare and I set up a joint email account for my dad's accounts, and a separate WhatsApp group just for LPA-related matters, so nothing gets lost among normal family messages. I also keep a notebook with a page for each account, noting details and who I've spoken to.
It's not that we don't trust each other, it just means we can hold each other to account and keep everything in one place.
My advice to others

I'd absolutely recommend getting an LPA. Most of us only turn to it once we're already in the middle of a difficult situation. For us, having it already set up meant we could step in and support our parents when the time came. We could just get on with it. That's what I'd say to anyone on the fence: get it sorted while things are calm, so it's simply there when you need it.”

Tracey is one of the many people across England and Wales who has taken on the role of attorney for a loved one. It's never too early to start the conversation about lasting powers of attorney with someone you trust at https://powerofattorney.campaign.gov.uk/

Felly, nid oes unrhyw beth yn cael ei golli ymysg negeseuon teuluol arferol. Rydw i hefyd yn cadw llyfr nodiadau gyda thudalen ar gyfer pob cyfrif, gan nodi manylion a gyda phwy rydw i wedi siarad.
Nid yw’n golygu nad ydym yn ymddiried yn ein gilydd. Mae’n golygu ein bod yn gallu dal ein gilydd i gyfrif a chadw popeth mewn un lle.
Fy nghyngor i eraill

Byddwn yn bendant yn argymell cael LPA. Dim ond pan fyddwn ni eisoes yng nghanol sefyllfa anodd y bydd y rhan fwyaf ohonom yn troi at ddefnyddio LPA. I ni, roedd ei sefydlu’n barod yn golygu y gallem gamu i mewn a chefnogi ein rhieni pan ddaeth yr amser. Roedden ni’n barod i fwrw ati’n syth. Dyna fyddwn i’n ei ddweud wrth unrhyw un mewn cyfyng gyngor: rhowch drefn ar bethau pan fydd pethau’n dawel, yna fydd popeth yn ei le pan fydd arnoch ei angen.”

Mae Tracey yn un o’r llu o bobl ledled Cymru a Lloegr sydd wedi ymgymryd â rôl atwrnai ar ran rhywun annwyl. Dydy hi byth yn rhy gynnar i siarad am atwrneiaeth arhosol gyda rhywun rydych chi’n ymddiried ynddo hagor o wybodaeth ar gael yn https://powerofattorney.campaign.gov.uk/

title: Shining a light on Campylobacter: a bright idea for safer food

content.content: Campylobacter is one of the leading causes of bacterial food poisoning in the United Kingdom (UK), with approximately 70,000 cases being diagnosed each year. This is likely an underrepresentation, as typically Campylobacteriosis only causes a self-limiting infection characterised with frequent diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and fever and may go unreported to health professionals. However, in England, 5-10% of cases require hospital care, with complications arising from the development of several post-acute infection syndromes such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, reactive arthritis, or bacteraemia.
Poultry is recognised as one of the principal sources of human Campylobacter infections, with transmission commonly occurring through the handling and consumption of contaminated poultry products.

Over the past two decades, the poultry industry has introduced numerous interventions, from on-farm biosecurity measures to improved hygiene and processing practices, aimed at reducing Campylobacter contamination throughout the food production chain. Despite these efforts, Campylobacter remains a persistent challenge for the poultry industry.

In conjunction with this, our routine surveillance of Campylobacter over the years has identified an increase in antimicrobial resistance to certain antibiotics used in the treatment of clinical human cases.
Together, the persistence of Campylobacter in the food chain and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance present an ongoing challenge to public health.

The relationship between food production and human health is central to the ‘One Health’ approach, which recognises that the health of people, animals, and the ecosystem is interconnected. Rather than considering these areas in isolation, One Health encourages collaboration across sectors to address shared health challenges.

In the case of Campylobacter, reducing bacterial contamination in poultry products could help lower the risk of human infection. However, achieving this has proven challenging, and no single intervention has been sufficient to eliminate the risk of Campylobacter infection in the UK.
But, what if one way to tackle these harmful bacteria was as simple as switching on a light?
Well, this may not be far from the truth.

Research carried out in collaboration between the Campylobacter National Reference Laboratory at APHA and Aidan Taylor’s group at the University of Reading has been investigating the use of violet-blue light to reduce Campylobacter contamination through a method called violet-blue photodynamic inactivation (VB-PDI). The additional advantage is that 405 nm light does not involve the use of ultraviolet (UV) radiation, potentially offering a more practical alternative for use in certain food-processing environments. However, appropriate safety assessments would still be required before introducing high-intensity lighting systems into workplaces.

Previous research has shown how effective VB-PDI is against laboratory strains of Campylobacter jejuni where they could achieve a 99.9% reduction in cell numbers within 2-minutes of exposure. This process works by activating naturally light sensitive molecules within bacterial cells, leading to the production of reactive oxygen species. These highly reactive chemicals can damage cellular components such as DNA or proteins, ultimately killing the bacteria.

However, while these findings were promising, several important questions remained. In particular, would VB-PDI be equally effective against the diverse range of Campylobacter species found in the poultry industry?

To investigate this, we selected 64 Campylobacter samples from three species that can cause illness in people: C. jejuni, C. coli and C. lari. These samples represented a wide range of genetic backgrounds and showed different levels of susceptibility to antimicrobial drugs.

Encouragingly, all 64 samples were susceptible to VB-PDI, with broadly similar responses regardless of species or antibiotic resistance. These findings suggest that violet-blue light could provide an effective means of reducing Campylobacter contamination across a diverse range of strains, including those resistant to antibiotics.
It is also pertinent that when developing a new technology, we as scientists ensure that we are not going to generate another problem for future generations to solve.

We have seen how the misuse of antibiotics and other bactericidal compounds can contribute to the development of resistance over time, meaning that infections are harder to tackle. Therefore, assessing how bacteria could develop resistance to violet-blue light is an important part of assessing its potential as a future intervention.

To investigate this, we repeatedly exposed Campylobacter strains to 405nm light, using conditions that killed 99% of the bacterial population. The surviving cells were then allowed to recover, before being treated again. This process was repeated 15 times to determine whether successive exposures could select for bacteria with increased tolerance. We observed no detectable increases in tolerance to VB-PDI. Although this does not rule out the possibility, it does provide encouraging evidence that repeated exposure may not readily select for increased tolerance.
So, what does this mean for the poultry industry?

The findings in this study raise the possibility of using VB-PDI as an additional tool to reduce Campylobacter contamination that may occur during poultry processing. In the future, we envisage specially designed lighting systems that may be implemented at various stages of the food production system, complementing or replacing existing food safety measures. However, further research is needed to establish how effectively this approach works on poultry products and in real processing environments. Factors such as treatment duration, light intensity, coverage of uneven surfaces, and the practical requirements of poultry processing would all need to be considered.

This research highlights the value of bringing together expertise in microbiology, veterinary surveillance and food safety. Through collaboration between APHA and the University of Reading, we have demonstrated that VB-PDI offers a promising approach to tackling Campylobacter, including strains resistant to clinically important antibiotics.

This innovation could provide a new way to tackle Campylobacter, one of the most common causes of food poisoning in people. By helping to prevent or control the bacteria in animals, it could reduce the amount of Campylobacter entering the food chain and therefore lower the risk of infection in people.

Better prevention could also mean less need for antibiotics to treat bacterial infections in both animals and humans. Reducing unnecessary antibiotic use is vital because overuse encourages bacteria to become resistant, making infections harder to treat (AMR).

The innovation therefore supports a One Health approach, recognising that the health of animals, people and the environment are closely connected. By tackling Campylobacter closer to its source, it has the potential to protect human health, improve food safety and contribute to the wider fight against AMR.

While further work is needed before this technology can be introduced into commercial settings, our findings represent an encouraging step towards developing additional tools for controlling foodborne bacteria. By combining innovative research with surveillance and collaboration across sectors, APHA continues to support a One Health approach to protecting people, animals and our shared environment.
Further information
Bembridge F, Whitmore JK, Ciesielski AM, Rodgers JD, Connelly SAM, Taylor AJ. (2026). One light to rule them all: photodynamic inactivation of diverse Campylobacter. Microbiology, 172.

description: This One Health Day, we shine a light on Campylobacter and explore how innovative research could protect our food, animals and people from harmful bacteria.

title: Creating tools for scaling generated content
authors: Pete Kowalczyk – Conversation Designer, GOV.UK AI team, GDS

content.content: In the GOV.UK AI team, we're working on personalised experiences that curate content for users based on their specific circumstances.
The potential value to users is huge, offering tailored interfaces that directly reflect their needs. But the content design challenge is a big one too. For example:

In this post, we look at some new design tooling we’ve made to evaluate and refine content quality at scale — and how this tooling helps us improve not only content but the design of our systems as a whole.
An example use case

One of our teams is currently working on guiding users through life moments by curating personalised plans. We’ve previously written about this work exploring using AI agents to curate tasks for users, create space for planning before action, and make work visible.These personalised plans might cover a scenario like having a baby, which involves multiple interactions with government that differ depending on circumstances. For example, a high income, married couple living in Scotland will need a different plan to a single parent claiming Universal Credit in England. The approach to generating these plans needs to accommodate a wide range of scenarios.
The team has designed these plans to contain multiple 'steps' and 'tasks' depending on what the user needs to do.
Each plan, step and task has been designed with its own content rules, such as:
These are the things a content designer would naturally define when working on static content.
The challenge is implementing them repeatably, at scale. When content is generated, it's not the content itself you're designing. It's the instructions that produce it.
What we've done to solve this

To measure content quality, we've built a test runner for our content instructions. Here’s how it works. We generate content, evaluate it, look at the failures, check the ones we disagree with, change the prompts where needed, and run it all again.It has four parts:
We use these content quality evals to assess the design of the content only. We have different systems for assuring accuracy, completeness, groundedness or faithfulness of the generated plans.

By turning our content rules into rubric criteria, we can make sure they are checked on every plan, every time.We can also measure what should not be there. Generated content tends towards too much: repeating a deadline that's already on the screen above, adding a caveat nobody asked for, being helpful in the wrong place. This tendency is easy to miss when you're reading one output and easier to catch when you're scoring hundreds.
Our tests also help to surface disagreements early. If "is this plain English?" fails on something we thought was fine, we can discuss it and amend the evaluation.
Regressions become visible too. For example, if we tweak a task prompt to fix one bad heading, we can see straight away whether that same tweak made titles longer everywhere else.
Responding to these evaluations

While generating and evaluating content, we can see where changes to the system prompts are needed. But tweaking prompts is only part of the work.When reviewing outputs, we can identify other opportunities to shape and improve the experience. For example, by improving the information architecture, changing the frontend design, and making system architecture choices such as the data schemas available to the models.

title: Behind the Food Hygiene Rating: The people making the scheme work
authors: Una Campbell, Senior Adviser (Hygiene) in Northern Ireland

content.content: This month, we celebrate 10 years of mandatory display of Food Hygiene Ratings in Northern Ireland.

We spoke to Una Campbell, Senior Adviser (Hygiene) at the Food Standards Agency (FSA) in Northern Ireland about her experience of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS). Una has worked as a district council Environmental Health Officer delivering the scheme on the ground, and as policy adviser on the scheme at the FSA.

When you visit a restaurant, café or takeaway in Northern Ireland, you'll probably recognise the familiar green and black Food Hygiene Rating sticker. But have you ever wondered what goes on behind the scenes to ensure the scheme provides people with information they can trust and confidence in the ratings they see?
Having experienced FHRS from two different perspectives, Una knows there's more to the scheme than the number displayed in a business window.
From carrying out inspections to supporting the scheme
Before joining the FSA, Una worked as an Environmental Health Officer (EHO) at Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon Borough Council, inspecting food businesses and their food hygiene standards.

"When I worked in a council, FHRS was very much part of the day-to-day job. My focus was on the individual food business: carrying out an unannounced inspection, assessing what I found and determining the appropriate rating."
"As any EHO who has delivered FHRS will know, that rating can be very important to a business. You see first-hand the impact it has and the importance businesses place on achieving a good rating."
Una was also working in local government when Northern Ireland moved from a voluntary Food Hygiene Rating Scheme to a statutory scheme with mandatory display in October 2016.
Ten years later, the scheme is well established with more than 99% of food businesses in Northern Ireland holding a rating of 3 or above and 84% achieving the highest rating of 5.
What does a Food Hygiene Rating actually tell you?
Food Hygiene Ratings are based on the standards found by an EHO during an inspection. Businesses are rated from 0 to 5, with a rating of 5 indicating very good food hygiene standards.
During an inspection, officers assess three key areas: how hygienically food is handled, the cleanliness and condition of the premises and how food safety is managed.

A Food Hygiene Rating isn't a review of how good the food tastes or the quality of service. It provides information about the hygiene standards found at the time of inspection, helping customers make informed choices about where they eat or order food.
For Una, having carried out those inspections herself provides an important perspective on the practical work involved in delivering the scheme.
"Having previously been one of the EHOs delivering FHRS in Northern Ireland, I still look at issues through an EHO lens but with my FSA hat on.
"If we’re considering an aspect of how the scheme operates, I’m usually thinking about how it will work in practice: is it clear, how will an officer apply it and what will it mean for the business?"
There's more behind the sticker than you might think
While EHOs are responsible for inspecting food businesses and determining ratings, the FSA also plays an important role in supporting the scheme.
FHRS is delivered through a partnership between the FSA and Northern Ireland's eleven district councils.

Council EHOs work directly with food businesses, while the FSA helps provide assurance and maintain consistency through activities including the annual food hygiene rating display audit and national consistency exercises.
For Una, moving to the FSA revealed another side of a scheme she already knew well.

“One of the biggest differences for me has been seeing just how much work goes on behind the scenes. It is not as simple as I thought. A consumer sees a 0 to 5 rating and the familiar green and black sticker, but there is a lot more behind it.

“An important part of that work is making sure accurate and timely information is available on the FHRS database, allowing consumers to check the rating of a food business online as well as at its premises.
"Working in the FSA I’ve come to realise and appreciate the importance of accurate and timely information being submitted to the FHRS database.

"For consumers to make informed choices, they need to be able to rely on the information they see, whether that is looking at the sticker when they arrive at the business or the rating they find when they check online."
Celebrating ten years of mandatory display

The Food Hygiene Rating Scheme was introduced in Northern Ireland in 2010 with mandatory display becoming a legal requirement in October 2016 under the Food Hygiene Rating Act (Northern Ireland) 2016.
The tenth anniversary is an opportunity to recognise the contribution of the food businesses, Environmental Health Officers, district councils and FSA colleagues who help make the scheme work.
It's also an opportunity to look ahead, as the way people buy and order food continues to change.

"Seeing the scheme from both sides has made me appreciate how the different roles contribute to the same purpose. Whether carrying out an inspection as an EHO or working to support and provide assurance around the scheme at the FSA, ultimately it is about helping consumers make informed choices and helping to protect public health."
Despite the change in role, Una hasn't forgotten what it's like to be on the other side of the partnership.
"I certainly haven’t forgotten what it is like to be the person walking through the door to do the inspection that ultimately determines that business’s Food Hygiene Rating."
Check before you choose
When choosing somewhere to eat or order food, look for the green and black sticker or check a business's rating online at food.gov.uk/ratings.
A Food Hygiene Rating tells you about the hygiene standards found at the time of inspection, helping you make an informed choice.

description: Interview with Una Campbell, a Senior Adviser (Hygiene) to celebrate 10 years of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme in Norther Ireland.

title: Farming and Food Partnership Board: Turning collaboration into action

content.content: The Farming & Food Partnership Board (FFPB) was established to bring together government and industry leaders to identify strategic ways to improve productivity, profitability and food security across the farming and food sectors.
Since its launch in March, the Board has focused on tackling barriers to growth and creating the conditions for greater investment and innovation.

Working with representatives from farming, food supply chain, retail and hospitality, the Board has considered where government and industry can work together most effectively.  This has focused on improving sector profitability and productivity in ways that support resilience and ensures economic and environmental outcomes can go hand in hand.

The Sector Growth Plans for horticulture and poultry are due to be published in 2027, with work continuing to be led by the sector expert groups. Through these plans, the Board has supported expert groups and supply-chain partners to develop evidence-based, market-led actions.
We will confirm plans for other Sector Growth Plans in due course.
This blog provides an update on the Board's recent work and sets out the actions that will now be taken forward to support growth across UK farming and food.
Priorities agreed at the October meeting

Planning and infrastructure, audit burdens and innovation were the focus of a package of action agreed for the poultry and horticulture sectors at the fourth Board meeting on 26 October. These actions aim to address practical barriers facing farm businesses.
The Board also endorsed proposals to tackle industry-wide challenges to building more farm reservoirs that will add water supply resilience.
Supporting growth in the poultry sector

Board members agreed for a joint working group, co-sponsored by Defra and the NFU, to conduct more work to address planning barriers affecting investment and growth in the poultry sector. This group’s work will support the development and delivery of the Poultry Sector Growth Plan.

The working group will act as a partnership between government and industry  on work that includes strengthening confidence in sustainable poultry litter management and equipping planning authorities to make informed decisions on new developments. Greater clarity in planning processes can help unlock investment in modern poultry facilities.
Members also agreed that close collaboration between industry, government and regulators will be essential to finding solutions that support both environmental outcomes and growth ambitions.
Reducing audit and championing R&D for horticulture
The Board considered evidence showing fresh produce growers face overlapping audits, creating significant administrative burdens and costs.

Members agreed that industry and retailers should continue work to reduce duplication and improve efficiency. It was agreed that effective audits are critical to maintaining standards, but that greater efficiency would help free up time and resources for growers, unlocking growth and productivity.

The British Retail Consortium agreed to convene a roundtable with sector representatives and retailers to maintain confidence in assurance processes while reducing unnecessary bureaucracy for producers and processors.

Putting growers at the heart of innovation was central to the sector-led proposals for a more coordinated approach to horticultural research and development discussed by the Board. This will create opportunities for collaborative investment across the whole supply chain. It will help accelerate the adoption of new technologies, automation, robotics and other innovations to improve productivity and resilience.
Improving water resilience through on-farm reservoirs

The Board agreed that action should continue at pace to make it easier for farmers to invest in water storage, improve flexibility for abstraction and strengthen resilience to future drought conditions. Members heard about efforts across government to address barriers to reservoir construction, including planning, regulation and financing.
Defra continues to work with MHCLG and other government departments to improve the policy and regulatory environment for on-farm reservoirs.
Next steps
Taken together, these measures can help create a more productive, resilient and competitive food and farming sector.
Focus now turns to delivery. Work is already underway to take forward the actions agreed by the Board.

The agreed actions cover poultry planning barriers, reducing audit burdens in horticulture, strengthening research and innovation proposals, and improving access to water infrastructure. Officials, industry representatives and sector experts will continue developing these actions.
The Board will continue to monitor progress and identify further opportunities where collaboration between government and industry can support growth across the food and farming sectors.
The joint statement and summary of minutes from the latest meeting are published on the FFPB GOV.UK page, alongside statements from previous meetings. The Board will meet next in early 2027.
We look forward to sharing further updates as this work progresses. Please subscribe to the Farming Blog so you don’t miss our next update.

title: The Representation of the People Bill – Lords committee stage

content.content: The Representation of the People Bill has now entered Lords Committee Stage in Parliament, where its measures will be examined in detail.
This is the next major step in changing the law to make these improvements. This stage of the Bill will also include amendments to implement the measures recommended in Rycroft Review.
The new laws will be in place in time for the next General Election.
What’s changing and why is it important to me?
Big changes are coming to the way elections work – and a once-in-a-generation change will allow 16 and 17-year-olds to get involved in democracy across the UK for the first time in history.

👩‍🎓 Young people get to vote – 16 and 17-year-olds across the UK are finally being given the right to vote in all elections. Electoral registration age is also being lowered to 14, so that 16-year-olds can vote even if an election happens on their birthday.
🪪 Making voting fairer and easier - Expanding the list of IDs allowed at polling stations, with UK-issued bank cards set to be accepted as voter ID.
🧾 Improving voter registration - to help more voters get registered, so their vote and their voice count in matters that affect them.

💷 Protecting our democracy from foreign money - Tough new rules to stop foreign and illegal money from being involved in our elections, protecting British voters and our democratic power on matters that affect us.
🚫 Putting a stop to harassment - Extra measures to protect political candidates, campaigners and staff who often face abuse
🧑‍⚖️ Stronger regulation - The people in charge of overseeing elections, the Electoral Commission, will get tougher powers to enforce all these rules.
This will make politics fairer, so every voice counts and every vote is protected ✅
And we’re going even further on improving voter registration 🗳️

To help more voters get registered we're making it easier to register. Today we're also publishing a prospectus which will invite local authorities to pilot how data can help them identify people who are not registered or have out of date information. This will eventually help us to test simple new ways for people to get their details on the electoral roll.

Our plans will mean fewer people miss out and less time is spent entering your details across different government websites, making it quicker and easier for every eligible voter to register to have their say in elections.
What about political finance changes?
Tackling foreign financial interference – the Rycroft Review measures 🗳️

The independent Rycroft Review looked at how foreign money could find its way into UK politics, and what needs to change to stop it. The government has accepted all of Rycroft's recommendations and is bringing many of them in through the Representation of the People Bill.
Measures in the Bill already include:

💰 A cap on donations from overseas electors – anyone eligible to vote from abroad will only be able to donate up to £100,000 a year to a political party, closing a loophole that let large sums flow in from people living outside the UK.

🏠 A "minimum residency" rule – if an individual based abroad moves back to the UK, they'll still be subject to the £100,000 cap until they've been living here for a full calendar year, so people can't dodge the rules simply by moving to the UK.
🪙 A ban on political donations made in crypto assets – stopping the anonymity of cryptocurrency being used as a back door for foreign or illegitimate money.

🏢 Tougher tests for company donations – businesses donating to political parties will need to show they have a genuine connection to the UK or Ireland, and the amount they can give will be judged against their profits rather than their revenue, so shell companies and inflated turnover can't be used to disguise foreign cash.
Residency test🏠
It's vital that those contributing to politics in the UK reside in this country, and that foreign money shouldn't be used to interfere in UK elections and politics.
Eligibility to make political donations over £100,000 is already based on donors being registered to vote as a resident in the UK, not overseas.
That's why we're also looking to introduce an enhanced residency test for political donors, so donors have to demonstrate an ongoing presence in the UK⏳.
We're working to introduce these measures as soon as possible, and further details will be set out in due course 📅.
🗳️ Why are these changes important to me?
Your vote is better protected from foreign interference, with tighter rules on donations and company funding. 🔒
16 and 17-year-olds get a say for the first time, bringing more young people into our democracy. 🙋
Registering to vote will be simpler, with less form-filling and new pilots helping councils find and register eligible voters. 📝
Every vote counts, and every vote is protected. ✅

title: Self-Care Week: Turning Health Awareness into Health Action

content.content: by Helen Donovan, M.Ed. BSc. RN, RHV, Queen’s Nurse, FRSPH. Self-Care Forum Chair. Independent nurse consultant and immunisation specialist nurse.

Public health campaigns have shaped the UK's health for nearly two centuries. From Victorian sanitation reforms to modern NHS initiatives, they have helped change behaviours, influence policy and improve lives. Their success comes from a consistent formula: clear messages, trusted messengers and practical actions repeated often enough to become habits.
That lesson remains important today.
Prevention shift

As the NHS seeks to shift from treating illness to preventing it, self-care has a critical role to play. The NHS 10-Year Health Plan sets out three major shifts: from sickness to prevention, from hospital to community, and from analogue to digital. It also emphasises personalised care, reducing health inequalities and helping people take a more active role in their health. These ambitions recognise that healthcare services alone cannot create a healthier nation.
Self-care is an essential part of the solution.

This is particularly true in adult social care, where maintaining the health and wellbeing of those receiving care and those providing it is vital. Supporting carers to look after their own physical and mental health is crucial, as an immunisation specialist nurse I would advise all carers to take up preventive measures such as seasonal flu vaccination.  It helps protect vulnerable people and reduces disruption to care in communities.
National Self-Care Week

National Self-Care Week, organised by the Self-Care Forum and taking place from 16-22 November 2026, provides an opportunity to promote the knowledge, confidence and skills people need to care for their physical and mental wellbeing. This year's theme is Mind & Body, reflecting the strong connection between mental and physical health and the role both play in helping people live well.
The importance of self-care is reinforced by findings from the Living Self-Care Survey, conducted by the Self-Care Forum and Imperial College London's SCARU.
People don’t recall public health recommendations

The research found that many people are unable to recall key public health recommendations, including guidance on physical activity and alcohol consumption. Importantly, the challenge is not simply a lack of information. Awareness does not always lead to action.

The survey also identified differences in self-care confidence across the population. Older adults reported higher confidence in their self-care knowledge, while people with disabilities and long-term conditions reported lower confidence. Financial pressures, lack of time and motivation were also barriers to practising self-care.

These findings highlight the importance of health literacy and the need for public health messages that are easy to understand, relevant and repeated consistently over time. As health services become increasingly personalised and digitally enabled, people need the confidence and skills to access, understand and use health information effectively.

This aligns closely with the NHS 10-Year Health Plan. Prevention depends on people having the knowledge and motivation to adopt healthier behaviours. Delivering more care in communities requires individuals to feel confident managing their health and long-term conditions.
Success is about more than just sharing information

History shows that successful public health campaigns do more than share information. They make healthy behaviours feel achievable and normal. Campaigns such as Smokefree, 5 A Day and flu vaccination programmes succeeded because they combined evidence-based messages with trusted local and national voices.

The same principles apply to self-care. Self-Care Week brings together health, social care, education, local government, workplaces and community organisations to promote healthier behaviours, improve health literacy and build confidence in self-care. Through simple actions and consistent messages, awareness can turn into action. Self-care is not "no care" - it is supported care, helping create healthier communities and supporting NHS ambitions for prevention and reducing health inequalities.

title: Helping young people explore STEM careers at Defra

content.content: When I was asked to support the SmartSTEMs Moray event, the brief sounded straightforward: run a workshop, explain the work of Defra and encourage young people to consider careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).

But rather than give a presentation, I wanted pupils to experience the collaborative problem-solving that often takes place across Defra. That idea became an immersive challenge: Can Your Team Keep Defra Running?
The scenario - creating an emergency response centre

I created a fictitious scenario that went something like this. Following reports of a fictional national sweet shortage, the pupils joined a Defra Emergency Response Team. Their task was to investigate clues, complete challenges and gather the information needed to save the nation’s sweets.
At the end of September 2026, my colleagues Keiran and Flora helped me transform a university lecture theatre in Moray into a fictional Defra Emergency Response Centre.
Around 50 pupils, aged 10 to 14, worked in teams across four challenge stations. Each pupil had an assigned role, and every activity called for collaboration, critical thinking and creativity.

After months of designing and testing the activities, I expected the challenges to keep everyone busy for some time. The pupils had other ideas. They solved problems so quickly that my carefully planned timings soon fell apart.
That gave us more time for something equally valuable: conversation.

Pupils asked what Defra does and whether they could work with animals, become scientists or pursue careers in technology and cyber security. We were able to show that Defra needs a wide range of people and skills, including environmental science, animal health, project delivery, digital and cyber professions.
Recognising different strengths
One moment stayed with me more than any puzzle or challenge.

As part of the exercise, the pupils were given different roles; what struck me was how seriously they embraced them. Each brought something different to the challenge, and some found confidence and purpose in parts of the exercise we might not have expected. It was a lovely reminder that giving young people different ways to contribute can bring out strengths we might not otherwise see.
After the final challenge, a pupil asked: “Do you think I could work for Defra one day?”
I said yes. Defra needs scientists, animal specialists, project managers, cyber professionals, analysts and people with many different strengths and perspectives.
Later, a member of the school support staff told me it was the happiest they had seen that pupil. It was that feedback that meant the most.
Building confidence in future talent

Investing in future talent is an important part of creating lasting social value. Outreach events do more than raise awareness of careers. They help young people recognise that their interests, abilities and perspectives have value, and that future opportunities can be achievable.

SmartSTEMs Moray also showed what partnerships between schools, universities and employers can achieve. By creating practical and engaging experiences, we can help young people build confidence, curiosity and awareness of the many routes into STEM.

If even one pupil left feeling more confident about their future because of a conversation that day, I would consider the mission a success. The nation’s sweets may have been rescued, but the real achievement was helping young people imagine what could be possible for them.
More information

title: Architecture is for everyone: designing better public services together
authors: Phil Rumens, Government Chief Architect, Government Digital Service

content.content: As I start my new role as Government Chief Architect, one of the questions I want us to think about is what it really means to be an architect for digital, data, or technology in the public sector and how architectural thinking can help us design better public services.
What does it mean to be an architect in government?

The official answer, from the Government Digital and Data Profession Capability Framework, is a professional role group focused on designing, structuring and aligning public sector capabilities, systems and data to deliver effective government services.

In practice, that means looking beyond any one service or system and asking how the pieces fit together, whether the technology, data and ways of working we've inherited are still serving the people who use them, and what needs to change if they're not. This wider view helps people across public services make better informed decisions, avoid solving problems in isolation and design services that work more effectively together.
Redesign, not renovate

Public services have often grown incrementally and without a joined-up design. A new system here, a workaround there, another layer added to keep things running. Renovating to deliver short-term improvements can only take us so far.
Like a building that's outlived the purpose it was designed for, the structure itself can often be the problem.
In some cases, redesign means knocking down walls to create a more joined-up approach, for example to share data, which is something the National Data Library is working on.

Data locked in unconnected systems, held under individual arrangements and described in separate ways makes it harder to deliver services that work for people, and harder to make good decisions. A more open plan approach but still locked in the confines of a secure environment works better.

In other cases, it means designing something new from the ground up, which is the approach of CustomerFirst. Starting from what people need, rather than from what the existing architecture can do, opens up different choices.

In both examples, this isn't about improving within the constraints of the current constructs. It’s about redesigning them so they can support joined-up public services that are simpler to access, easier to navigate and better able to respond to people’s needs.
Architecture is for everyone

In September we ran our first cross public sector architects community event,  “Architects Assemble”, hosted by the Local Government association, and one thing came across loud and clear; the design of new architecture isn't limited to people with “Architect" in their job title.

Service designers, developers, product managers, data specialists, delivery leads and policy colleagues all make decisions that shape how a service fits together.  Frontline workers also have an important part to play, bringing real-world insight into where the connections between technology, data and services could be improved.
Every choice about how data is stored, which components to reuse or how a service connects to others is an architectural decision, whether or not it happens to be labelled as one.

This the approach GDS Local is taking with co-creating the Local Government Architecture Model, with people working in councils, government departments and the private sector all contributing, and we continue to build out and iterate it, to make it even more useful for those who use it.

Working in this way also gives practitioners the opportunity to learn from others facing similar challenges, share approaches that have worked, build connections across organisational boundaries and contribute to how architecture practice develops across the public sector.

So, architecture works best as a shared responsibility, with a common language and a shared understanding of what good looks like, not something done by a specialist team alone and handed over but co-created with the teams that use it.
Shared responsibility, specialist expertise
None of this means the specialist roles go away. We'll always need people whose job is to see the big picture and build firm foundations.

Enterprise, solution and technical architects and others in the profession, who can see across organisational boundaries, spot dependencies and duplication, and make the case for long-term coherence when short-term pressures pull the other way.
Specialists help teams apply architectural thinking consistently and effectively.

They can provide the patterns, standards and guidance that make good decisions easier, and challenge and support teams on the trade-offs, and it’s why the Government Digital Service published an Architectural Decision Record Framework, to establish the practice of documenting architectural decisions across teams, programmes, and organisations.

Making architecture everyone's business needs strong specialists to help it work. That's what we mean by “Architects Assemble”: bringing together the people who contribute to architectural thinking, with the expertise and leadership of the architecture profession at its heart.
Help shape architecture across government
If we're serious about designing better, more joined-up public services, we need to bring together the people who shape the services, technology and data they rely on.

That's why we're building Architects Assemble, a community bringing together architects and others involved in architectural thinking from across the public sector. Whether you're an architect by profession or your work contributes to architectural decisions, the community is a place to connect with others facing similar challenges, share experience and expertise, and learn from approaches being developed across government.

Through events, webinars and other opportunities to connect, the community will help practitioners build stronger relationships across organisational boundaries, discuss common challenges and contribute to how architecture practice develops across the public sector.
Our next webinar takes place on Tuesday 3 November 2026, 11am to 12.30pm, providing an opportunity to hear more, connect with others and get involved in the conversation.
If you'd like to be part of the community and help shape what comes next, register your interest in joining Architects Assemble.

description: Architecture is for everyone. Whether you're a developer, service designer, policymaker or architect by profession, the decisions you make help shape how public services work. By bringing people together across disciplines, we can share expertise, challenge assumptions and build the foundations for better, more joined-up public services.

title: Building major infrastructure that leaves nature better off

content.content: New reservoirs, energy networks, roads and railways will help shape the country for decades to come. They also offer an opportunity to restore habitats and create more space for wildlife – from new wetlands to connected corridors where nature can thrive.
Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) turns that opportunity into a measurable commitment.

From today, 2 November 2026, developers applying for a Development Consent Order (DCO) for nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIPs) in England must ensure their project delivers at least a 10% net gain in biodiversity.

For NSIP developers, this brings a consistent framework for building nature recovery into these much needed infrastructure projects from the outset. For nature, it means major infrastructure will contribute to lasting landscape-scale habitat improvements.
A consistent framework with flexibility for NSIP developers

The framework builds on the experience of infrastructure providers already delivering BNG voluntarily. It gives developers a consistent set of requirements to plan against, with flexibility to deliver biodiversity gains on site, off site or through a combination of both.

The approach is tailored to major infrastructure. Requirements focus on habitats affected by development, rather than the whole development site, with a simpler approach for qualifying temporary impacts. It delivers on recommendations from the Nuclear Regulatory Taskforce Review, led by John Fingleton, for a streamlined BNG framework that supports infrastructure delivery and nature recovery.
Developed through extensive engagement with industry and the environmental sector, the BNG framework is supported by guidance to help applicants, advisers and decision-makers apply the requirements.
What NSIP developers need to do
NSIP developers should consider BNG from the earliest stages of project design, alongside other environmental requirements, and engage early with ecologists and relevant stakeholders.
Early planning helps developers identify opportunities to avoid habitat loss, incorporate improvements into scheme design and plan the long-term management needed to deliver them.
DCO applications must include an outline biodiversity gain plan explaining how the project will achieve at least 10% BNG, supported by a biodiversity metric calculation.

Developers must follow the biodiversity gain statement relevant to their project, to meet the mandatory requirements. Our guidance for NSIP developers provides further detail on the steps to take through design, consenting and delivery.
Lasting benefits for nature and communities

For major infrastructure, BNG offers opportunities to restore land, create wetlands and connect habitats so wildlife can move through the landscape. These improvements can contribute to wider nature recovery ambitions and the government’s environmental targets.

To ensure lasting benefits for wildlife, significant on-site habitat gains and off-site gains must be legally secured, managed and monitored for at least 30 years. On-site gains can be secured through DCO requirements, planning obligations or conservation covenants.
Depending on how they are designed and managed, habitat improvements can also help manage flood risk, store carbon, improve air and water quality, and provide greener surroundings for communities.
Extending mandatory BNG to NSIPs is also expected to generate additional demand for biodiversity units, supporting the off-site market.
Industry voices welcome mandatory BNG for NSIPs
Julia Baker, Global Submarket Lead for Biodiversity and Nature at Mott MacDonald, said:

“Mandatory biodiversity net gain is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for major infrastructure to help restore nature while delivering lasting benefits for communities. The focus now must be on making BNG an integral part of infrastructure design and long-term management, rather than simply a requirement to meet”.
Kat Stanhope, Strategic BNG Manager at National Grid, said:
“[This] is an important step forward for both nature recovery and the delivery of critical infrastructure.

“As we build the network Britain needs for its energy future, which will include a large number of Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects, BNG offers an opportunity to create lasting value for people and the environment, at scale, supporting more resilient landscapes, thriving habitats and benefits for local communities alongside the infrastructure the country needs.”

Sally Hayns, CEO of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management (CIEEM), said: “From today, leaving nature better off becomes a condition of consent for major infrastructure projects.
“This is a 'build once, benefit twice' approach we welcome: wildlife corridors alongside power lines, new wetlands at reservoirs and rich habitats along new railways.
“This is the future of nature restoration at scale, and ecologists across the country are on the ground ready to apply Biodiversity Net Gain to our biggest builds - where the biggest gains lie.

“Early ecological input will be essential to seize the opportunities: more climate-resilient development, thriving nature markets, better flood management and greener surroundings for local communities.”
Tom Clancy, Head of Environmental Delivery, National Highways, said:

“We welcome the introduction of mandatory biodiversity net gain for Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects. Implementing voluntary BNG across our major enhancement portfolio to date has resulted in improved optioneering and design decisions that have better outcomes for nature and communities.”
Next steps

We will continue working with Natural England, the Planning Inspectorate, the Planning Advisory Service, local authorities and other stakeholders to support a smooth transition to mandatory BNG for NSIPs and help developers put the framework into practice.
